Hello,

I'm really interested in getting into fountain pens. I seriously have found a new hobby. I love to hand write and I love to collect vintage things, so it would be a great thing to get into. I have absolutely no idea where to start. Is there anything specific? What got you into fountain pens?
How'd you get into fountain pens?

Hi there, Glad you are looking into the hobby! As far as where to start, I'm planning to add some more beginner's resources to the sidebar soon, but for now you might find the "Fountain Pens 101" playlist on Goulet Pen's YouTube channel and some of the earlier videos on SBRE Brown's channel (both linked in the sidebar) helpful. Is there anything specific? Well...yes. But you don't need to worry about too much right away. Start by figuring out your budget for your first pen, then look around the retailers that are listed in the side bar and see what you like (I know that you said that you want to collect vintage things, but I would suggest that you make your first pen or two a new one to give yourself time to learn the ropes and study up on vintage pens). Once you have a short list, stop back here and see what people have to say about the pens that you are considering. I would really start with the 101 videos though as they will familiarize you with the terminology, explain nib sizes, and a multitude of different things much better than I can. After that you can start to think about ink, which is a whole separate rabbit hole :) .

This is a great hobby and I hope you decide to get started. Please post any questions that you have here, this is a very inviting community and everyone, including myself and the rest of the mod team love to help newcomers.

edit: I got into FPs after finding an old Eversharp in my grandmother's desk. It hadn't been used in years and wasn't functional but it sparked something in me and I bought my first pen, a Pelikan M200 the next day. I've been using FPs almost exclusively for about five years now.

Also, here's some FP porn to entice you further. Be aware that there was custom work done to the nib of that Namiki Falcon (the flex pen) so don't expect to be able to get that kind of line variation from most pens.
Thank you so much for the resources and information! I'm so pumped about this!
No problem! Be sure to report back with your new pen (and get you some flair!)

I've always enjoyed Stationery, I remember when I got my first job and got to go check out the stationery cabinet. So many boxes of pens and paper and erasers, oh my! While on a business trip to San Fran I bought an Ohto F-Spirit from a pen store. A cheap way in but it was a start. Then a coworker and I started discussing our love of fountain pens and the next thing I knew I was buying more pens and we were comparing and contrasting the various brands.

My recommendation to start is to save up a bit and get a mid range pen. Something between $30 and $50 and a bottle or two of ink. If you start too cheap then it will be frustrating, all the cheap pens I've gotten Jinhaos and my Ohto, even the Pilot Metro have been okay at best. but the $30 to $60 pens have been great, my Sheaffer 100, TWSBI Diamond 580 and Lamy Safari are just good consistent writers with little maintenance.

I'd recommend also going into a pen shop and trying out some of the pens. Any reputable pen shop should be happy to let you dip into some ink and write a few lines. The grip and the way the nib feels to you is important!

Thanks for the advice. I also dig stationary. I think my main motivation for wanting to get into fountain pens is so that I can write letters to people on stationary. Reinventing the use of snail mail.
Yeah, I am thinking of getting into that too but for now I keep a journal. Feel free to check out /v/penpals if you're looking to write letters :)

I agree about starting with a decent pen; you don't really appreciate how smooth and pleasurable the writing can be with any of the pens under $20, even the Pilot Metropolitan (as Nofrill said). I would add the Faber Castell Loom to the list of recommended starter pens, and would also suggest "upgrading" to a Lamy Al Star instead of a Lamy Safari—they are the same pen essentially, except the Al Star has an aluminum body while the Safari has a plastic one; the Al Star is more substantial in the hand.

Your ink selection is almost as important as your pen selection, maybe more important, because it's easy to get a good pen but hard to get a good ink right for you—how do you want to express yourself in color? Or in stark black? Is color-fastness, waterproof-ness, etc. important to you? Just some things to think about... If you want to "cheat," stick with a premium brand like J. Herbin or Pilot or Pelikan, maybe a brand that offers standard international cartridges. Then, when you get more comfortable with expressing yourself through shading, saturation, etc. you can branch out to more "niche" inks.
